title: Mystery Drawing

paragraphs.text: On January 30, 1998, an art auction was held in New York city. One drawing was of a pretty girl, but it attracted little attention. The catalogue listed the work as a German drawing done in ink and with coloured chalk, dating back to the early 19th century, with styling borrowed from the much earlier Renaissance period. A New York dealer, Kate Ganz, purchased the picture for $21,850. The price had barely changed almost ten years later when a Canadian collector, Peter Silverman, bought it. The drawing might actually date from the Renaissance, he thought. Ganz herself had mentioned Leonardo da Vinci as an influence on the artist. Silverman wondered whether it was the work of the great Leonardo himself, but discovery of a Da Vinci is truly rare. At the time of Silverman’s purchase, it had been more than 75 years since the last authentication of one of the artist’s paintings. It had never been recorded that Da Vinci ever made a major work like this, and neither were there any known copies. If this image was an authentic Leonardo, where had it been hiding for 500 years?

Silverman emailed a digital image of the drawing to Martin Kemp, professor of art history at Oxford University and renowned Leonardo scholar. Kemp immediately flew to Zurich, where Silverman kept the drawing in a bank vault. Kemp was excited and began his own investigation. He was aided by Pascal Cotte of Lumiere Technology in Paris, who used high resolution multispectral scans which allowed Kemp to study the drawing’s different layers. The more Kemp looked, the more he saw what he considered evidence of Leonardo’s hand: the beautiful tone of the colours, the precise lines, and the fact that the shaded areas showed distinctive strokes just like Leonardo’s. The subject’s expression was self-confident but thoughtful. She appeared to be someone growing up too fast, and conveyed Leonardo’s belief that a portrait should reveal ‘motion of the mind’.

Kemp also needed proof that the portrait had been made during Leonardo’s lifetime (1452– 1519) and that its historical details fitted the artist’s biography. Material analysis strongly suggested that the artist had used calfskin, quite normal for the time, and this was carbon-dated. Its origin was placed somewhere between 1440 and 1650. Then costume research revealed that the girl belonged specifically to the Milanese court of the 1490s, with its fashion for elaborately bound hair. Leonardo lived in Milan during this time, accepting commissions for portraits of people in the royal court. Stitch marks on the edge of the 3 portraits suggested that it came from a book, possibly the sort, common at the time, that would commemorate a royal marriage.

Kemp’s detective work led him to a name, Bianca Sforza. A daughter of the Duke of Milan, she was married in 1496 to Galeazzo Sanseverino, commander of the Milanese troops and a patron of Leonardo’s. Tragically, she died a few months later. In 2010 Kemp and Cotte published their findings in a book. Several prominent Leonardo scholars agreed, others were sceptical. The possibility of a high-quality forgery was raised. Doubt centred around the drawing’s sudden, almost miraculous appearance. Where had it come from? Kemp didn’t know. Then, quite unexpectedly, a message came from David Wright, professor of art history at the University of South Florida. Having followed the very public dispute, Wright suggested to Kemp, whom he had never met, that his answer might lie in the National Library of Poland in Warsaw, inside a book called the Sforziad. Wright, an expert on Renaissance iconography, described it as a commemorative volume for the marriage of Bianca Sforza, a suitable occasion for a Leonardo portrait.

Kemp and Cotte travelled to Warsaw. Cotte’s macrophotography revealed that a page had been removed from the exact place in the Sforziad where a portrait might have been added. The moment arrived when they inserted a copy of Blanca’s portrait into the open book. It fitted perfectly. For Kemp, this was the proof. It was a single portrait by Leonardo that had gone into a book and then onto a shelf.

According to Wright, the volume reached Poland in the early 1500s, when a member of the Sforza family married a Polish royal. The page was removed, possibly at the time of the book’s rebinding in the 17th or 18th century. The trail grows fainter here. What is known is that at some point it was acquired by an Italian man, a specialist in art restoration, and that his widow put it up for sale at auction.

These are amazing times for Leonardo admirers. Recently, London’s National Gallery exhibited Leonardo’s painting of Jesus Christ holding a globe, a work lost for centuries. In Florence, researchers looking for Leonardo’s Battle of Anghiari, last seen in the mid–1500s, are using technology to find out if the painting might be hidden behind a wall in the Palazzo Vecchio, but the issue has not yet been resolved.

Authenticating a centuries-old artwork is seldom an objective process. Ego, personal taste, and fear of legal cases all contribute to the judgement. To reach wider consensus, Kemp sent his latest findings to a number of leading specialists, almost all of whom declined to comment. Agreement ‘will take time’, concedes Kemp, ‘but I have clear confidence in the research we’ve done. One thing is sure, should the day come when Bianca Sforza’s face hangs in a museum as a true Leonardo, everyone will stare.’
